overview:
The fighting began in the winter of 2014, in the vacuum left when Ukraine's president Viktor Yanukovych fled Kyiv after months of protest over his refusal to sign an association agreement with the European Union. Within days, soldiers without insignia — later acknowledged by Moscow as Russian troops — took the Crimean parliament, airports and military bases, and a hastily staged referendum was used to justify annexation in March. It was the first time since the Second World War that one European state had seized and absorbed the territory of another. Over the following weeks armed groups declared "people's republics" in Donetsk and Luhansk, and a war settled into the coal and steel country of the Donbas: Russian-backed forces stiffened by Russian equipment, volunteers and, at moments of Ukrainian advance, regular Russian units. Two agreements signed at Minsk in 2014 and 2015 stopped the largest battles without resolving anything, and the line froze into trenches. Roughly fourteen thousand people died there before 2022.

That long, low-intensity phase ended on 24 February 2022, when Russia invaded across the northern, eastern and southern borders in an attempt to take Kyiv and replace the government. The attempt failed within weeks, and the war became a grinding contest over the east and south — Bucha, Bakhmut, Sievierodonetsk, Lysychansk, Mariupol — fought with artillery, drones and long-range missiles, and accompanied by strikes on railway stations, shopping centres and the power grid. Millions left the country; millions more were displaced inside it. As of mid-2026 the UN human rights monitoring mission had verified at least 16,431 civilians killed and 48,613 injured since the full-scale invasion, and said the true figures are certainly higher; military losses on both sides run into the hundreds of thousands and are not reliably known.

The war reshaped things well beyond Ukraine. It ended Europe's dependence on Russian pipeline gas, brought Finland and Sweden into NATO, drove the largest Western arms transfers since the Cold War and made drones the defining weapon of contemporary land warfare. Negotiations have repeatedly been attempted — US-mediated talks, short truces in 2026 — without producing a settlement, largely because Moscow continues to demand all of the Donbas, including the portion of Donetsk province Ukraine still holds. At the time of writing the fighting continues.
significance: More than any event since 1991, this war broke the assumption that borders in Europe were settled and that large-scale interstate conquest belonged to the past. It forced a continent that had spent thirty years demobilising to rearm, redrew the energy map of Eurasia, pushed Russia into deep economic and political dependence on China, and turned Ukraine — a country whose separate national identity Moscow has repeatedly denied — into something consolidated by the attempt to erase it. It also became the first war in which cheap drones, commercial satellite imagery and open-source verification shaped both the fighting and the world's ability to watch it, a template every military since has studied.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, the Council on Foreign Relations backgrounder, and UN human rights monitoring reporting from July 2026; the dataset's sixteen events are heavily weighted toward named battles of 2022 in the Donbas and hold almost nothing on 2015–2021, on Crimea and the occupied territories after annexation, or on the war's economic and diplomatic dimensions. Casualty and territorial figures are contested and incomplete everywhere: the UN verifies only what it can reach, Russian-occupied areas are largely closed to independent monitoring, and both governments treat their own military losses as state secrets. Because the war is ongoing, anything written about its current phase dates quickly.
